newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Dec personal income shows vigorous economy.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Dec personal income shows vigorous economy.

text.p: December U.S. personal income and consumption data, as expected, showed wages benefitted from a tighter labor market and that a steady rate of spending helped fuel robust economic growth in the fourth quarter, analysts said.
"It's just another sign that as 1996 came to a close, the economy was operating in a rather vigorous fashion," said Kevin Flanagan, economist at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc.
"You continue to see wage gains and that has been a byproduct of the tightening in the labor force."

The Commerce Department said income from wages, salaries and all other sources rose 0.8 percent in December, its fastest rate in six months. Meanwhile, personal spending increased 0.5 percent. Both figures matched the consensus forecasts from a Reuter poll of economists.

The November income figure was upwardly revised to a 0.6 percent increase from a previously reported 0.5 percent gain, while spending was downwardly revised to 0.4 percent increase from a prior 0.5 percent rise.

Economists said the data will have little to no impact on the outcome of the Federal Open Market Committee's February 4-5 meeting, which the marketplace widely expects to yield no change in official interest rates.

"The (Federal Reserve) looks at it, but mainly from a forecasting perspective because it's a derived statistic -- it lies on top of the December employment and retail sales data we already saw released," said Cary Leahey, senior economist at Lehman Government Securities Inc. "It just tells you that 1996 ended on a good, solid note, which we already saw in Friday's (fourth quarter gross domestic product) release.
Dean Witter's Flanagan said the income and spending report would have "no impact" on Fed policymakers.
The data did not prompt the economists interviewed to adjust their GDP forecasts for the first quarter of 1997, which already relied on the continuation of solid consumer spending.

"Consumption continues to be a supporting influence to the economy as a whole and as long as incomes and confidence continue to stay at levels we've been seeing, I wouldn't expect to see any major pullback in consumer spending," Flanagan said.

Domestic debt and equity markets showed little reaction to the data. Treasuries slipped a few ticks, with most players sidelined until the scheduled 1000 EST/1500 GMT release of the National Association of Purchasing Management's report.
In early morning trade, the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond fell 7/32 at 96.04/32 to yield 6.80 percent. The Dow Jones industrial average had slipped 28 points at 6784.
